summary: Describes Vouch By Reference, a protocol that adds third-party certification to email. Independent parties can vouch for the owner of the domain name tied to received mail, helping receivers decide how much to trust the sender.

plainLanguage.summary: Vouch By Reference lets an independent company vouch for the owner of a domain that sent you an email. The sender names the vouching company in a header field, and the company publishes its answer in the DNS. You look the answer up and decide whether to trust it.

questions: how does vbr certify email senders
how does vbr use dns txt records
what does mc=transaction mean in vbr
subtitle: Lets a third party vouch for the owner of a sending domain, so a mail receiver can check it over DNS.

tldr.problem: Email receivers can tell that a message was signed, but not who is behind the domain that signed it. Without that, a receiver has to trust the sender's own claim about who will vouch for it.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a VBR-Info header field naming the domain, the type of message and the certification services it believes will vouch for it. The receiver checks the domain with DKIM, DomainKeys, SPF or Sender ID, then asks the vouching service over DNS whether it vouches for that domain and that type of message.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from April 2009 and was later updated by RFC 8553. The vouching service carries real power, so the receiver must pick which services it trusts.

facts.label: Header parameters
facts.value: md, mc and mv; all mandatory

today: RFC 5518 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2009. It was later updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: What VBR Adds to Email
sections.content:
Vouch By Reference, or VBR, is a protocol for adding third-party certification to email. It permits independent third parties to certify the owner of a domain name that is associated with received mail. VBR may be performed anywhere along the email transit path, by any capable receiving module, either within the handling service or by end-user software.

The protocol has two parts. In the first, the sender affixes VBR information to mail messages, saying which domain certification services the sender believes will vouch for mail associated with that sender. In the second, the receiver queries one or more certification services to obtain information about the identity associated with a received message, and this second protocol uses the DNS to distribute the certification information.

The sender performs two steps: it adds a VBR-Info header field to its message, and it protects the message as appropriate. A prerequisite for successful VBR operation is validation of the identity associated with the message, because VBR is based on the use of domain names as identifiers. The RFC warns that a receiver who uses the results of vouching to adjust spam scores is placing a great deal of operational trust and power in the vouching service, so such a receiver needs to select services with care and may want more than one to avoid a single point of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Email tells you that a message was signed, but not who is behind the domain that signed it. VBR adds a way for an outside company to vouch for that domain, and for you to check the vouch over DNS.

sections.title: How a Receiver Checks a Claim
sections.content:
A message receiver uses VBR to determine certification status by following four steps. It extracts the domain to certify and the type of message content. It verifies legitimate use of that domain using one or more authentication mechanisms. It obtains the name of a vouching service that it trusts, either from among the set supplied by the sender or from a locally defined set of preferred vouching services. Finally it queries the vouching service to determine whether that service actually vouches for that type of content for that domain.

The receiver compares the list in the message with the list of services it trusts and queries each service that appears in both. A message may carry more than one VBR-Info header field, and in the terminology of the mail format RFC 5322 it is a trace header field, so it SHOULD be added at the top of the header fields. When a message has several VBR-Info fields, verifiers SHOULD check each in turn or in parallel until either a satisfactory certifier is found or all the header fields have been checked. All VBR-Info fields in a single message MUST have identical mc= values.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a claim, the receiver takes the domain and the kind of mail from the header, proves that the sender really controls the domain, picks a vouching service it trusts, and asks that service whether the claim holds.

sections.title: The VBR-Info Header Field
sections.content:
The VBR-Info header field has the format VBR-Info: md=<domain>; mc=<type-string>; mv=<certifier-list>;. The domain is the domain for which vouching is offered, the type string is the content type of the message, and the certifier list is a list of domain names of certification providers that the sender asserts will vouch for this particular message. The certifier list is one or more domain names with a colon between each, and the elements must not contain any white space.

For example, a signer with two companies willing to vouch for its transactional notices adds VBR-Info: md=somebank.example; mc=transaction; mv=certifier-a.example:certifier-b.example; to the header of its outgoing message. All three header parameters are mandatory, and in particular there is no default for the md= domain. Upper and lowercase characters are equivalent, although conventionally the contents are all in lower case. For upward compatibility, verifiers MUST accept the fields in any order and SHOULD ignore any fields other than the three defined here.

The formal syntax is given in ABNF: vbr-info-header = "VBR-Info:" 1*([FWS] element [FWS] ";"), where each element is an md=, mc= or mv= element, and the type string is one of all, list or transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: The header field holds three values: the domain being certified, the kind of message, and the certification services the sender says will vouch for it. All three must be present, and a receiver must accept them in any order.

sections.title: The DNS Lookup
sections.content:
For each service on both the message's list and the receiver's trusted list, the receiver marshals a domain name to look up, built from three DNS labels, from left to right: the domain name that asserts it can be certified, the literal string _vouch, and the host name of the vouching service. It queries that name for a DNS TXT record, looking it up in exactly the same manner as any other domain name. For a message signed by somebank.example, the receiver might look up somebank.example._vouch.certifier-b.example or somebank.example._vouch.certifier-a.example.

If the TXT record exists, it contains a space-delimited list of all the types that the service certifies, given as lowercase ASCII. A record might read transaction list. The receiver then checks whether either all or transaction appears, since all means the certifier vouches for every message type sent by that domain. The receiver needs to ignore services it does not trust, otherwise a bad actor could add an authority it controls and vouch for itself.

The name _vouch was chosen because any domain name that includes it as one of its labels cannot be a valid host name, so there is never accidental overlap. If the reply holds several character-strings, the code handling it MUST assemble them into a single one before any syntactic verification, and MUST then check that the record consists of strings of lowercase letters separated by spaces, discarding records in any other format. This defends against misconfigured records and against irrelevant records synthesized from DNS wildcards. The VBR record MUST have only one TXT record. The RFC notes that this method relies on the efficiency, reliability and experience of the existing DNS, that the lookup is very efficient, that certifiers can add and delete client records quickly, and that the lookup also uses the DNS's negative caching.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer lives in the DNS. The receiver looks up a name built from the domain, the word _vouch and the vouching service's host name. The TXT record it finds there lists the kinds of mail the service vouches for.

sections.title: Types of Message Content
sections.content:
The RFC defines three types of content for which a certifier can vouch, and notes that describing the content of mail messages is inherently open to interpretation, so these definitions can be read in very different ways by different people. The value in the mc= element is self-asserted and its purpose is auditing. A sender may have a certifier for transactional mail but not for advertising mail, and might be tempted to mislabel advertising as transactional; the mc= element creates the audit trail that lets certifiers catch such cheating and remove the certification.

all means all mail from the sender. list is the category for email sent to multiple recipients where each piece of mail is identical or very similar to the others. transaction is the category for transactional messages, which are a response to a specific action of the user or a notice about an event in the user's account at the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: A certifier can vouch for all of a sender's mail, for mailing-list style mail, or for transactional mail that responds to something the user did. The sender names which kind it is claiming, and the certifier's record says what it actually vouches for.

sections.title: Getting a Trustworthy Domain Name
sections.content:
VBR relies on having a domain name that identifies the party accountable for the message, which requires obtaining the domain name and holding a strong basis for believing its use is valid, that is, that it has not been spoofed. Senders SHOULD use DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), and MAY use DomainKeys, the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) or Sender ID.

With DKIM, the md= value MUST match the domain name taken from one of the DKIM-Signature header fields: the domain from the i= field if the signature has one, otherwise the domain from the d= field. The VBR-Info header field SHOULD be included in the set of header fields protected by DKIM, so that a malicious party cannot change it or add bogus VBR-Info fields, and it SHOULD be added in the header immediately below the corresponding DKIM-Signature header field. With DomainKeys, the md= value MUST be the same as the domain name in the d= parameter of the DomainKey-Signature header field, with the same protections recommended. With SPF, the md= value MUST be the same as the domain name in the reverse-path address that is the first parameter to the SMTP MAIL command, and the domain is valid only when the SPF process produces a "pass" result. With Sender ID, the md= value MUST be the same as the domain name in the Purported Responsible Address in the message, and again the domain is valid only when the process produces a "pass" result.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain in the claim has to be one the sender really controls. The RFC prefers DKIM for that, and also allows DomainKeys, SPF or Sender ID, each with its own rule for which domain name counts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VBR is used to let users trust independent third parties to certify the owner of a domain name associated with received mail. The party validating the mail might use that trust relationship to perform actions that affect the security of its system, so the receiver of a message with a VBR-Info header field MUST ignore certifiers that it does not trust. Otherwise a bad actor could just add an authority that it has set up so that it can vouch for itself.

Implementations SHOULD also limit the number of VBR-Info header fields they process in a single message, in order to protect themselves from a make-work or denial-of-service attack. A message can carry several VBR-Info fields, and each one costs a lookup and a set of comparisons, so an unbounded number of them is a way to waste a receiver's work.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver must ignore any vouching service it does not trust, or an attacker could vouch for itself. It should also cap how many VBR-Info headers it processes in one message, so that a flood of them cannot waste its time.
